title: What dispatch skips: static and private methods

blocks.text: Only **non-static, non-private** methods are virtual. A static method with the same signature in a subclass **hides** the superclass's one: a call is bound at compile time to the declared type. A private method is never dispatched: a subclass method with the same name is a different method.

items: `Base.kind()` returns `"base"`, and `Derived` overrides it to return `"derived"`.
`Base.label()` is **static** and returns `"Base"`; `Derived.label()` is **static** and returns `"Derived"` (it hides `Base.label()`).
`Virtuals.kindOf(Base b)` returns the kind of the object `b` refers to, whatever the declared type.

`Base.introduce()` returns `"I am " + secret()`, where `Base.secret()` is **private** and returns `"base"`. `Derived` has its **own private** `secret()` returning `"derived"`. Keep both helpers private.

blocks.text:
new Base().kind()          -> "base"
Base.label()               -> "Base"
Derived.label()            -> "Derived"
Base b = new Derived();
kindOf(b)                  -> "derived"
b.introduce()              -> "I am base"

cases.says: kind() answers with each object's own class, and each class's static label() names its own class.
kindOf, given a Derived through a Base reference, reports "derived", because it asks the object rather than a static method.
introduce() on a Derived still uses Base's private secret(), because private methods are never dispatched.

concepts: Private methods are never dispatched dynamically: a subclass method with the same name is a separate method.
A static method with the same signature in a subclass hides the superclass's one, and a call to it is bound to the declared type.
